Brief Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency department and was 
evaluated by the orthopedic surgery team. The patient was found 
to have a left valgus impacted femoral neck fracture and was 
admitted to the orthopedic surgery service. The patient was 
taken to the operating room on ___ for left closed reduction 
and percutaneous pinning of hip, which the patient tolerated 
well. For full details of the procedure please see the 
separately dictated operative report. The patient was taken from 
the OR to the PACU in stable condition and after satisfactory 
recovery from anesthesia was transferred to the floor. The 
patient was initially given IV fluids and IV pain medications, 
and progressed to a regular diet and oral medications by POD#1. 
The patient was given ___ antibiotics and 
anticoagulation per routine. The patient's home medications were 
continued throughout this hospitalization. The patient worked 
with ___ who determined that discharge to home with services was 
appropriate. The ___ hospital course was otherwise 
unremarkable.

At the time of discharge the patient's pain was well controlled 
with oral medications, incisions were clean/dry/intact, and the 
patient was voiding/moving bowels spontaneously. The patient is  
weightbearing as tolerated in the left lower extremity, and will 
be discharged on Lovenox for DVT prophylaxis. The patient will 
follow up with Dr. ___ routine. A thorough discussion 
was had with the patient regarding the diagnosis and expected 
post-discharge course including reasons to call the office or 
return to the hospital, and all questions were answered. The 
patient was also given written instructions concerning 
precautionary instructions and the appropriate follow-up care. 
The patient expressed readiness for discharge.

LLE: Incision well approximated. Dressing clean and dry. Fires 
FHL, ___, TA, GCS. SILT ___ n distributions. 1+ DP

Discharge Instructions:
INSTRUCTIONS AFTER ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY:

- You were in the hospital for orthopedic surgery. It is normal 
to feel tired or "washed out" after surgery, and this feeling 
should improve over the first few days to week. 
- Resume your regular activities as tolerated, but please follow 
your weight bearing precautions strictly at all times.

ACTIVITY AND WEIGHT BEARING:
- Weightbearing as tolerated left lower extremity

MEDICATIONS:
  1)  Take Tylenol ___ every 6 hours around the clock. This is 
an over the counter medication.
  2)  Add oxycodone as needed for increased pain. Aim to wean 
off this medication in 1 week or sooner.  This is an example on 
how to wean down:
Take 1 tablet every 3 hours as needed x 1 day,
then 1 tablet every 4 hours as needed x 1 day,
then 1 tablet every 6 hours as needed x 1 day,
then 1 tablet every 8 hours as needed x 2 days, 
then 1 tablet every 12 hours as needed x 1 day,
then 1 tablet every before bedtime as needed x 1 day.  
Then continue with Tylenol for pain.
  3)  Do not stop the Tylenol until you are off of the narcotic 
medication.
  4)  Per state regulations, we are limited in the amount of 
narcotics we can prescribe. If you require more, you must 
contact the office to set up an appointment because we cannot 
refill this type of pain medication over the phone. 
  5)  Narcotic pain relievers can cause constipation, so you 
should drink eight 8oz glasses of water daily and continue 
following the bowel regimen as stated on your medication 
prescription list. These meds (senna, colace, miralax) are over 
the counter and may be obtained at any pharmacy.
  6)  Do not drink alcohol, drive a motor vehicle, or operate 
machinery while taking narcotic pain relievers.
  7)  Please take all medications as prescribed by your 
physicians at discharge.
  8)  Continue all home medications unless specifically 
instructed to stop by your surgeon.
      
ANTICOAGULATION:
- Please take  Lovenox daily for 4 weeks
 
Followup Instructions:
___

Large areas of skin tears - across bilateral shoulders, right 
upper posterior ribcage, right arm including forearm elbow and 
upper arm; right posterior trochanter, right knee. Right arm has 
full-thickness skin tear, no active bleeding.

Small laceration on right lower leg is sutured and superior to 
this the wound is approximated with steri strips.

Drainage from all wounds is small serosanguinous. There are no 
signs of infection.

Coccyx with 1 cm red-based partial thickness ulcer, also present

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ came to the ___ ___ 
Department on ___ after falling down ___ stairs while at 
home two days prior to presentation. He had gone to an outside 
hospital, but was transferred to ___ due to extensive skin 
tears on his back, right arm and right leg. CT head to pelvis 
was negative for other injuries. Plain films were done of his 
right upper extremity and right lower extremity and all were 
negative for fractures or dislocations.

On admission, the patient's wounds were bleeding and his INR was 
1.9 due to the coumadin he takes for his atrial fibrillation.  
We stopped his coumadin because the extensive tearing and easy 
friability of his kin led to some concern for the possibility of 
coumadin-induced skin necrosis (although we were aware he had 
been taking the coumadin for quite some time). Additionally, his 
daughter reports that he has had a recent history of frequent 
falls, and we were concerned about keeping someone with a high 
fall risk anticoagulated.

The plastic surgery team evaluated Mr. ___ and did not feel 
that his wounds were amenable to skin grafting, however, they 
would like him to follow-up in their outpatient clinic for 
further evaluation (the appointment has been scheduled and is 
included in his discharge paperwork). For wound management, they 
recommended adaptic dressings changed every other day for his 
right arm. 

The wound care team evalauted Mr. ___ as well. They 
recommended daily dressing changes for all other wounds 
(excluding the right arm) and daily cleansing with a wound 
cleansing solution.

Physical therapy has been working with Mr. ___ since his 
admission in an effort to prevent deconditioning and evaluate 
his physical therapy needs.  They noted that he has decreased 
step length and an unsteady gait during ambulation with 
increased ant/post sway, but no gross loss of balance.  

Mr. ___ attributes his falls to loss of balance secondary to 
decreased sensation of his lower extremities bilaterally. He 
does have a history of diabetes, but he says the peripheral 
neuropathy is a side effect from chemotherapy he had several 
years ago for treatment of lymphoma.

During this admission we called Mr. ___ outpatient 
cardiologist to discuss the possibility of taking him off 
Coumadin permanently. We believe his history of falling puts him 
at high risk of a serious bleed if he remains anticoagulated. 
After talking with the outpatient cardiologist, the decision was 
made to discharge him without coumadin, and to address his 
anticoagulation options in his follow-up appointment with his 
cardiologist next week.

Since his admission, Mr. ___ has been eating a regular diet, 
taking his home medications (except for the coumadin), and has 
not required IV hydration. His pain has been well-controlled 
(with 0.5-1 mg PO oxycodone prn) and has only been a issue 
during dressing changes.

He is currently stable and no longer requires acute inpatient 
care. In addition to discharging Mr. ___ to an extended care 
faciltiy for management of his wound care, we have also 
scheduled his follow-up appointments with his cardiologist, his 
primary care physician and with plastic surgery.

Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any questions, 
concerns, or need additional details concerning his hospital 
course.

7. Metoprolol Succinate XL 12.5 mg PO DAILY 
 
Discharge Disposition:
Extended Care
 
Facility:
___
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Extensive skin abrasions on right arm and back; smaller abrasion 
right lower leg.

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - requires assistance or aid (walker 
or cane).

 
Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to ___ after 
you fell down stairs while at home. You sustained extensive skin 
abrasions on your right arm, back, and leg. You were managed 
conservativelt, i.e. without any surgery, and you are now ready 
to be discharged to an extended care facility for wound 
management.

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*Your pain is getting worse or changes location.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any new symptoms that concern you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. 

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Incision Care:
*Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner if you have 
increased pain, swelling, redness, or drainage from your wounds.
*Avoid swimming and baths until your follow-up appointment.

It was a pleasure taking care of you during your hospital stay 
and we look forward to seeing you at your follow-up visit in the 
Trauma / Acute Care Surgery clinic.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is an ___ year old man with history of celiac 
disease, hypertension, history of pulmonary embolism, a fib, 
osteoporosis, and gallstone pancreatitis who presented with 
elevated WBC/fever/elevated lactate/diarrhea/ARF.  Each of the 
problems addressed during this hospitalization are described in 
detail below: 
.
# colitis/GI bleeding: Pt admitted to ICU with sepsis (Febrile, 
tachycardic, leukocytosis, bandemia (bands 37 on admission),  
elevated lactate). Based on the clinical presentation, recent 
Abx course, there was a high suspicion of C. diff colitis, 
although other etiologies such as other infectious etilogies, 
ischemic colitis given atrial fibrillation, cholangitis, 
refractory celiac disease were considered.  No evidence of 
colitis was present on abd CT scan, although this was a 
noncontrast study.  The patient was pan-cultured and started on 
antibiotic regimen including PO Vanco, Flagyl, and Zosyn. A 
number of other studies were sent including fecal culture, ova 
and parasites, C. diff, Yersenia, Shigella, Campylobacter, 
Microsporidia, Giardia, Cryptosporidium were sent and were 
negative. The patient was kept NPO, put on TPN.  Aggressive 
fluid resuscitation was given.  C. diff toxins were negative x 4 
and PO Vancomycin was discontinued on ___.  The patient was 
seen by GI service, who recommended continuing Abx treatment 
with IV Vanc, Zosyn, Flagyl and contacting ERCP to discuss 
follow-up of the biliary stent placed on ___. On transfer to 
the floor, the pt continued to have persistent leukocytosis and 
diarrhea.  The ID team was consulted to discontinue Zosyn given 
that his picture was consistent with colitis.  On ___, the pt 
underwent a flexible sigmoidoscopy which revealed a friable, 
ulcerative colonic mucosa which was concerning for viral 
pathologies such as CMV.  He was empirically changed to PO 
vancomycin for concern of severe C diff and started on 
ganciclovir for empiric CMV coverage.  A serum CMV viral load 
was sent and was negative.  Pathology of colon biopsies was 
consistent with colitis, inflammation.  CMV stains on path were 
negative as well.    
.
Though all C diff and CMV studies have returned negative, a 
decision was made with GI and ID teams' input to continue both 
oral vanco and ganciclovir treatment, though Vancomycin PO was 
d/c'd on ___ as cdiff was negative X6.  Though his clinical 
picture seemed to fit C diff (colitis, diarrhea, leukocytosis) 
his diarrhea seemed to improve when ganciclovir was initiated.  
With the completely negative infectious results, there was also 
some strong concern that this event may have been ischemic 
colitis as the patint also has evidence of embolic infarcts in 
his brain and has atrial fibrillation, so the decision was made 
to restart the patient on coumadin with a heparin bridge. 
.
___. Patient then had approximately 5 bowel movements 
from 0300 to 0600  passing marroon stools with clots. His HCT 
was 21.1 on morning labs on ___ and was transferred to 
the ICU.
.
While in the ICU he receieved 3U of blood and had a negative 
bleeding scan.  He was started on IV PPI and changed back to 
home medication on ___.  His Hct remained stable and he had a 
brown stool the morning of transfer back to the floor.  A repeat 
Flex sig ___ showed good healing of the colonic lesions so 
anticoagulation was restarted. 
.
On ___ his diarrhea began to worsen again. ID and GI were 
called back to re-examine and another infectious w/u was 
initiated, but was again unrevealing. An EGD was performed and 2 
gastric ulcers were found and biopsies of the small intestine 
were done in multiple places to r/o MALT. These results showed 
celiac sprue, with MALT stain pending at the time of discharge. 
He was started on loperamide for symptomatic improvement which 
worked well and should be titrated to ___ BM's per day.
.
At the time of discharge the patient had been receiving 
loperamide and was down to ___ BM per day, but was having some 
increasing abd distention. Plan is to hold all loperamide and 
restart if BM frequencies increase. Need pathology f/u as well. 
Need f/u HCT checks and monitoring for s/s of significant 
bleeding. ___ require intermittant transfusion if HCT drifts 
down as it has been slowly decreasing over last 2 weeks with 
blood draws and possibly slow loss from GI source. Would 
consider transfusion for HCT<24.   
.
# MRSA bacteremia - On ___ blood culture bottles grew 
MRSA.  IV Vanco started and PICC line discontinued ___ for 
suspicion that it was the source of the infection.  ID was 
consulted and recommended ordering a TTE which was negative for 
valvular vegetations.  He had a new PICC line placed on the 
right UE on ___.  After further review of his case (hx 
endocarditis ___, as well as possible renal infarcts on CT 
scan).
.
PICC removed on ___ and surveillance blood cultures since 
admission have been without growth. PICC tip was sent for 
culture on ___ and has final result of no growth. TTE on 
___ was negative for valvular vegetations; however, could 
not rule out small vegetations. Patient has a past history of 
endocarditis in ___, which increases his risk for recurrent 
endocarditis and ID consult recommending TEE, which was negative 
for vegetations on ___.  He received a total of 4 weeks of 
Vancomycin per the ID team, and completed this on ___. At the 
time of discharge he has a left tunnelled catheter. His 
discharge was held for a day b/c of a clogged line which cleared 
with TPA held in the line for 2 hours then drawn out. There has 
never been any problems flushing the line, just drawing labs 
back. Patient is a difficult peripheral stick, but can be done 
if needed.  
.
# UTI - Urinalysis and culture was drawn on ___ due to 
concern for low grade temperatures and a rising leukocytosis at 
that time. As U/A was unimpressive, treatment decision hinged on 
a urine culture that was positive for enterobacter on 
___. Ciprofloxacin IV was started at that time on ___.  
Repeat urine cultures ___ and ___ were negative for 
enterobacter, but positive for enterococcus.  Per ID a repeat UA 
was performed and was negative for nitrites and leuk esterase.  
The ID recommended discontinuing ciprofloxacin ___ since the 
enterbacter had cleared and did NOT want to treat the 
enterococcus (VRE), since this is likely now a colonizer (UA was 
negative).
.
# RUE swelling - pt noted to have some RUE edema approximately 
___.  A RUE US revealed no flow in a portion of cephalic vein, 
likely representing a superficial vein clot.  Due to the ongoing 
need for PICC line for TPN as well as other indications for 
anticoagulation (Afib with hx embolic strokes), heparin gtt was 
entertained, but was not started given his falling Hct and 
guaiac positive stools.  On ___, the pt went for an ___ guided 
tunnelled line and had his PICC removed.  His RUE swelling is 
slowly resolving.  However, the tunneled line had to be removed 
(see below).
.
* Biliary stent - The inpatient GI service recommended that ERCP 
be contacted in order to determine how to manage his biliary 
stent in the setting of a rising lipase.  The team felt that the 
stent had not migrated, but did agree that the stent would need 
to be removed.  The ERCP team removed the stent on ___ 
without complication.
 . 
* Acute on chronic kidney disease (Stage II): On admission, 
creatinine was noted to be 3.8 up from baseline of 0.6. It was 
believed to be prerenal and secondary to severe dehydration. 
With aggressive hydration, his Cr declined back to normal.
.
* Anion gap acidosis ___ lactic acidosis and uremia - This was 
thought secondary to his severe colitis and MRSA bacteremia.  
His anion gap was resolved at the time of transfer to the floor.
.
* Supratherapeutic INR on admission - Secondary to both coumadin 
and poor PO intake.  Vitamin K given in ICU and coumadin/ASA was 
held given diarrhea and guaiac positive stools.  The patient 
received additional IV Vitamin K as INR on the day of callout 
was 4.5.  His INR improved and was 1.5 on the ___.  Given his 
atrial fibrillation and subacute strokes and renal infarct, ASA 
was restarted on ___ and then stopped in the setting of GIB.  
There is strong indication for re-anticoagulation to be 
initiated at lower dose and carefully monitored. Discussion 
undertaken with patient, daughter and PCP after careful review 
of ___ outside neurology consult report.  Pros and cons 
presented to patient. Anticoag held until repeat Flex Sig was 
done ___, and tunnel line placed ___ then restarted. 
His goal INR should be ___ with ideal range ___ given his high 
bleeding risk.

* Atrial fibrillation with hx embolic strokes: On admission, his 
ASA and coumadin were held.  At ___, he had complained of 
visual changes and he had a neurology consultation and was found 
to have subacute strokes - bilateral posterior infarcts (right 
side affecting posterior temporal and occipital lobes; left side 
involving medial right occipital lobe).  He was restarted on 
coumadin at Kindred at 5mg QHS but had supratherapeutic INRT.  
On admission, ASA and coumadin were both held.  His CT Abd 
revealed a new renal infarct, may be related to embolic 
phenomenon from Afib vs. endocarditis.  His ASA was restarted on 
___ then held in the setting of GIB, which was felt to be due 
to ischemic colitis (other evidence for embolization).  He was 
started on Diltiazem on ___ then changed to his home 
metoprolol on ___.  Neurology consult was cancelled in light of 
pt refusal, and fact that there is strong indication to 
anticaogulate with careful monitoring. Full discussion with pt 
and his daughter and he agreed.  As above, coumadin restarted 
___ and INR should be check frequently. would no restart 
aspirin at this time.
 . 
* Transaminitis - Likely related to hypoperfusion from severe 
diarrhea.  Had resolved at time of transfer to the floor.  Of 
note, pt had  biliary stent placed ___ and after further 
discussion with ERCP was removed.
.
* Celiac disease: Has refractory disease and had been on TPN for 
the past ___ years per his outpatient GI attending.  Held 
intermittant with above complication, but has been restarted 
without event. The patient will require that all medications be 
confirmed with the manufacturing company that they are gluten 
free before he will agree to take them.  He has some of his own 
meds to take that he know is gluten free.  
.  
* Benign hypertension:  Some of his BP medications were held in 
the setting of septicemia picture in the ICU.  He slowly was 
restarted on his home metoprolol. The calcium channel blocker 
and ACEI was no longer needed.  
.
* Hypothyroidism: Continued Levothyroxine. thyroid labs checked. 
 
.
* History of PE:  S/p course of coumadin in past, but now back 
on anyway for AFib reasons and h/o embolic phenomenon.
.
* Osteoporosis: Home D2 50,000 units on ___ and ___, 
citracal + D 315-200 units BID were continued.
.

Name:  ___.                Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___

Chief Complaint:
Orthostasis
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
None
(Had laminectomy and fusion ___ and was discharged ___ 
came back from rehab same day for orthostatic hypotension)

 
History of Present Illness:
 Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with a PMH lumbar and  
 cervical spondylosis, cervicogenic headaches receiving botox  
 injections, h/o lung and breast cancern s/p resection, HTN, 
CRF,  
 scleroderma/CREST who presented for a laminectomy and fusion 
due to bilateral lower extremity pain and difficulty with 
walking. She underwent L2 laminectomy and non instrumented 
fusion on ___ with Dr. ___.  
 In speaking with the patient, she reports that the symptoms 
that led her to pursue this elective surgery were these attacks 
of severe lower extremity pain, often association with a 
sensation of pain in her thighs, and attacks where her legs 
would "give out." She also reports chronic urinary incontinence 
which acknowledgement that this may or may not improve with the 
lumbar surgery as above, but was hopeful that the surgery may 
offer additional benefit.  
 She reports that her postoperative course yesterday was notable 
for a similar attack of lower back pain and the sensation of her 
legs given out to cause a mechanical fall. Today when she rose 
to stand, she felt lightheaded, which led to the obtaining of 
orthostatic vital signs which were positive. She had some blood 
loss during her surgery and is receiving 1 unit PRBC today. 
During the episode of lightheadedness, she denies chest pain, 
shortness of breath, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting. She 
reports good oral and liquid intake. She denies dysuria or 
changes in urination. She states that today her post operative 
pain has been the worse. She also endorses constipation and has 
not had a bowel movement since the surgery.  
 In review of her medications, she is on a large amount of 
antihypertensives as well as torsemide 60 mg daily. These home 
medications were continued. She reports that she thinks she 
takes the torsemide for "kidney problems," but endorses chronic 
lower extremity edema which is worse. She also endorses a 
chronic headache lasting ___ years.  
 ROS:  
 (+) Per HPI  
 (-) Denied cough, shortness of breath. Denied chest pain. 
Denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain. No recent 
change in bladder habits. No dysuria.

ABDOMEN: Soft, not distended, nontender. +BS.

NEURO: Moving all extremities equally against gravity. Face

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ yo woman with h/o lung and breast CA s/p 
resection, CREST syndrome, CKD, spinal stenosis recently 
admitted for laminectomy and fusion ___, with course c/b 
orthostasis, discharged but re-admitted to medicine for further 
management of orthostasis and pain, who was noted to have new 
SVT and AF for which she was started on beta blocker and 
anticoagulation.

# NEW SUPRAVENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA with 
# NEW ATRIAL FIBRILLATION: The patient has no known history of 
arrhythmia. On ___ ___, she felt weak in her legs while moving 
to commode. On commode she appeared to be less responsive. She 
was noted to have pulse of 220 and SBP of 68 and was moved back 
to bed where she denied lightheadedness, dizziness, confusion, 
chest pain, dyspnea. On EKG she was noted to have SVT not 
responsive to vagal maneuvers (carotid massage, bearing down). 
Cardiology was called and adenosine was administered, which 
revealed an underlying rhythm of sinus with PACs. She was put on 
telemetry overnight and per EP there was concern for underlying 
AF, making her not a likely candidate for ablation. She was 
started on metoprolol 12.5mg TID but had persistent SVT runs 
(asymptomatic) and was increased to 25mg TID which resulted in 
few to no SVT bursts. She was discharged on 75mg metoprolol XL. 
Orthopedics was consulted about starting systemic 
anticoagulation; they determined that her recent surgery was not 
a contraindication, so she was started on Apixaban.  Risks and 
benefits of anticoagulation were discussed at length. TSH was 
normal. (Of note, her XR verapamil for CREST was fractionated 
the day the SVT was discovered to try and minimize orthostatics 
(see below); this is not thought to have contributed to the 
arrhythmia, but it cannot be certain, and she was returned to 
her XR dose the next day). She was discharged on ___ of 
Hearts Monitor for 2 weeks with follow up with instructions to 
follow up with Dr. ___ in ___ weeks. 

# ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION in the setting of
# HYPERTENSION: The patient was discharged initially from 
surgery despite orthostatic hypotension with symptoms, on her 
home torsemide and losartan. On re-admission a brief infecitous 
workup was performed (low suspicion) and was notable for 
negative UA/UCx and CXR without focal consolidation. Her 
orthoastics improved on hospital day 2 with IV fluids and 
holding of her torsemide and losartan. She did have ongoing 
hypertension to 160s-170s, so a half-dose of her losartan was 
started on day of discharge with good response. 

# CHRONIC HEADACHES
# LOWER BACK PAIN in setting of 
# SPINAL STENOSIS s/p DECOMPRESSION AND FUSION: This was 
difficult to control, but as her kidney function normalized to 
0.7-1.2 (per patient, due to discontinuation of Celebrex), we 
were able to discontinue her gabapentin, and obtained excellent 
pain control (per patient) with gabapentin 200/200/600mg in 
addition to TID oxycontin 10mg and acetaminophen 1000mg 
standing. Lidocaine patches on her anterior thighs were helpful. 
She used intermittent 5mg oxycodone q6h PRN, especially 
before/after ___. We were in touch with her outpatient pain 
provider ___. Of note, pain has a significant anxiety 
component as it is worse at night when there is nothing to 
distract her. 

# ABDOMINAL PAIN due to 
# CONSTIPATION: On admission, had not stooled since pre-op ___ 
at least). Bowel regimen was optimized and she stooled by 
hospital day ___. Discharged on increased dose of standing Senna 
with additional PRN of polyetyhtlene glycol, in addition to home

because you had anemia and kidney damage. You had many tests 
done in the hospital to find out why you had these changes in 
your labs.

finasteride and tamsulosin to treat the BPH. You were also given 
antibiotics to treat a urinary tract infection.

hospital.

vomiting, or diarrhea, please call your PCP and seek medical 
care.

Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___
 
Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: NEUROSURGERY
 
Allergies: 
Iodine and Iodide Containing Products
 
Attending: ___.
 
Chief Complaint:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
___ Right VP shunt placement

 
History of Present Illness:
Ms. ___ is a ___ yo F with NPH who presents today for elective 
Right VP shunt placement 
 
Past Medical History:
HTN, HLD, GERD, NPH, IBS 
 
Social History:
___
Family History:
Per OMR:  Brother died of colon cancer and a sister has coronary 
artery disease.  Her father died of colon cancer and also may 
have had small strokes.

 
Physical Exam:
Upon admission: 
alert & oriented x3 
PERRL 
MAE ___ 
No drift 

Upon discharge: 
AAO x 3
PERRL, EOMs intact
No drift, full strength and sensation throughout.
 
Pertinent Results:
___ CT head without contrast:
1.  Right VPS shunt terminates in the right anterior horn.  No 
pneumocephalus or hemorrhage. 
  
2.  Stable mild bilateral enlargement of the lateral ventricles 
including 
temporal horns since ___. 

 
Brief Hospital Course:
Mrs. ___ was admitted for placement of a right VPS. The 
procedure was well tolerated. A programmable valve was placed. 
She was transferred to the PACU after the procedure. A CT post 
operatively revealed that there was no hemorrhage and the shunt 
was in good placement.  The patient was transferred to the 
inpatient ward for further management and observation.

On post-op day 1, Mrs. ___ was recovering well.  Her pain was 
managed with narcotic and non-narcotic analgesics.  Her VP shunt 
setting was changed from 0.5 to 1.5 and the setting was verified 
twice.  Mrs. ___ was tolerating a regular diet and voiding 
without issue.  She was ambulating independently.

On the evening of ___, Mrs. ___ was discharged in the care of 
her husband.  At the time of discharge, she was afebrile, 
hemodynamically and neurologically intact.  Per discharge 
instructions, the patient should follow up in ___ days in the 
___ clinic for a wound check/staple removal.  Also, 
Mrs. ___ should also follow up with Dr. ___ in four weeks 
with a non-contrast head CT prior to that appointment.
 
Medications on Admission:
Diltiazem hcl, lisinopril, simvastatin, mirabegron, omeprazole, 
sertraline, antiox #10, aspirin (on hold before procedure)

 
Discharge Medications:
1. Acetaminophen 325-650 mg PO Q6H:PRN fever or pain 
2. Diltiazem Extended-Release 240 mg PO DAILY 
3. Docusate Sodium 100 mg PO BID 
4. Lisinopril 10 mg PO DAILY 
5. mirabegron 50 mg oral daily 
6. Omeprazole 40 mg PO DAILY 
7. OxycoDONE (Immediate Release)  ___ mg PO Q4H:PRN pain 
RX *oxycodone 5 mg ___ tablet(s) by mouth every four (4) hours 
Disp #*60 Tablet Refills:*0
8. Sertraline 100 mg PO DAILY 

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.
 
Discharge Instructions:
VP Shunt Placement:

You had a VP shunt placed for normal pressure hydrocephalus. 
Your incisions should be kept dry until the sutures are removed.
Your shunt is a ___ Strata Valve which is programmable. 
This will need to be readjusted after all MRIs or exposure to 
large magnets.  Your shunt is programmed to 1.5. 
It is best to keep your incision open to air but it is ok to 
cover it when outside. 
Call your surgeon if there are any signs of infection like 
redness, fever, or drainage. 

Activity
We recommend that you avoid heavy lifting, running, climbing, 
or other strenuous exercise until your follow-up appointment.
You make take leisurely walks and slowly increase your 
activity at your own pace once you are symptom free at rest. 
___ try to do too much all at once.
No driving while taking any narcotic or sedating medication. 
If you experienced a seizure while admitted, you are NOT 
allowed to drive by law. 
No contact sports until cleared by your neurosurgeon. You 
should avoid contact sports for 6 months. 

Medications
Please do NOT take any blood thinning medication (Ibuprofen, 
Plavix, Coumadin) until cleared by the neurosurgeon. 
       You may resume your daily aspirin on ___.
You may use Acetaminophen (Tylenol) for minor discomfort if 
you are not otherwise restricted from taking this medication.

What You ___ Experience:
Headache or pain along your incision. 
Some neck tenderness along the shunt tubing.
Constipation is common. Be sure to drink plenty of fluids and 
eat a high-fiber diet. If you are taking narcotics (prescription 
pain medications), try an over-the-counter stool softener.

When to Call Your Doctor at ___ for:
Severe pain, swelling, redness or drainage from the incision 
site. 
Fever greater than 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit
Nausea and/or vomiting
Extreme sleepiness and not being able to stay awake
Severe headaches not relieved by pain relievers
Seizures
Any new problems with your vision or ability to speak
Weakness or changes in sensation in your face, arms, or leg

Call ___ and go to the nearest Emergency Room if you experience 
any of the following:
Sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm, or leg
Sudden confusion or trouble speaking or understanding
Sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance or 
coordination
Sudden severe headaches with no known reason
 
Followup Instructions:
___

Back Pain

History of Present Illness:
Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with history of T11 fracture 
s/p kyphoplasty (___) and VP shunt for normal pressure 
hydrocephalus (___) who presents with acute on chronic low back 
pain.  
 
 The history was taken from the patient and her husband.  
 Her husband shares that about 3 days prior to presentation she 
woke up in the morning with total back pain, that then localized 
to the bilateral lower back. The pain was so bad that she was 
having trouble getting out of bed to walk or go to the bathroom. 
She had no leg pain or change in sensation of her legs, no new 
urinary incontinence (per husband has occasional urge 
incontinence) and no fecal retention or incontinence. On further 
questioning her husband says she ___ urinated much in the 
past few days, and associates this with her not wanting to use a 
bedpan. Because the pain was not improving, her husband brought 
her to ___. However, ___ referred her to ___ 
___ because their MRI wasn't capable of adjusting for her VP 
shunt.  
 In the ED, initial VS were: 97.1 (spiked to 100.9) 57 ___ 97% 
RA. On exam she had ___ bilateral hip flexion/extension, ___ 
bilateral ___ plantar and dorsiflexion, lumbar tenderness and 
normal rectal tone. Labs showed WBC 11.2, Cr 1.9 (0.8 in 
___, Na 129, lactate 1.1. CXR showed congestion and 
atelectasis. MRI brain showed no evidence of acute infarct, 
hemorrhage. MRA neck showed patent vessels; right V4 appeared 
diminutive. MRI T and L spine showed prior 
compression/kyphoplasty site, no lumbar spine cord signal 
abnormality, moderate to severe spinal canal narrowing at 
"L2-L3, L3-L4, L4-L5 due to a combination of disc protrusion and 
ligamentum flavum hypertrophy." She was given 1L IVF, 1 g IV 
ceftriaxone, Ativan 0.5 mg PO, oxycodone 5 mg- acetaminophen 325 
mg, and dilaudid 0.5 mg IV. Neurosurgery was consulted; VPS 
shunt was interrogated and set to 0.5. There were no further 
recommendations.  
 On arrival to the floor, patient's husband provides the above 
HPI and the patient agrees. She says she currently feels warm 
and that her pain was well controlled with the medication she 
was given in the ED. She, however, does not provide too much 
detail independent of her husband and answers in short word 
sentences. Per her husband, she does not have a history of 
multiple hospitalizations, frequent infections, or "kidney 
problems." When asked her functional status at baseline, he said 
"pretty independent."  
 Her husband adds that a few weeks ago she also had right eye 
visual deficits that lasted a few hours and went away. He says 
she had this a few years ago and no cause was found.  
 
Past Medical History:
HTN, HLD, GERD, NPH, IBS

___

Per OMR:  Brother died of colon cancer and a sister has coronary

MICROBIOLOGY

IMAGING:
___ CXR
The tip of a new right PICC line projects over the upper right 
atrium,
approximately 1 cm beyond the cavoatrial junction.  There is a 
partially
visualized right-sided ventriculoperitoneal shunt catheter.
There is minimal bibasilar atelectasis and unchanged pulmonary 
vascular
congestion.  No focal consolidation, pleural effusion or 
pneumothorax is
identified.  The size of the cardiac silhouette is within normal 
limits.  The
patient is post prior vertebroplasty of T11.
IMPRESSION: 
The tip of a new right PICC line projects over the upper right 
atrium,
approximately 1 cm beyond the cavoatrial junction.  No 
pneumothorax.

___ TEE
LEFT ATRIUM (LA)/PULMONARY VEINS: No spontaneous echo contrast 
or thrombus in ___.
RIGHT ATRIUM (RA)/INTERATRIAL SEPTUM/INFERIOR VENA CAVA (IVC): 
No atrial septal
defect by 2D/color Doppler.
AORTIC VALVE (AV): Mildly thickend (3) leaflets. No 
mass/vegetation. No abscess.
MITRAL VALVE (MV): Mild thickening leaflets. No systolic 
prolapse. No mass/vegetation. No abscess.
Mild [1+] regurgitation.
TRICUSPID VALVE (TV): Mildly thickened leaflets. No 
mass/vegetation. No abscess. Trivial regurgitation.
ADDITIONAL FINDINGS: 3D Imaging rendering with interpretation 
and reporting with image post
processing under concurrent supervision; requiring image on 
independent workstation. Time-out completed
per ___ policy: Non-operative Universal Protocol @ ___ 
13:23. TEE not feasible
without conscious sedation. Risks, benefits and alternatives 
were discussed and Informed consent was
obtained from the patient who desired to proceed. With rhythm, 
blood pressure and oxygen saturation
monitors, constant nursing observation, and direct attending 
supervision, the patient received an appropriate
level of sedation (see medication list above). The attending was 
at the bedside continuously for 16
min during sedation. The patient was subsequently observed with 
serial examinations until the return of
their gag reflex and presedation mental status. The TEE probe 
was placed into the esophagus under cardiology
attending supervision. No TEE related complications.

___ CT ABD/PELVIS
LOWER CHEST: There are trace pleural effusions with mild 
adjacent atelectasis.
The visualized lower lungs otherwise clear.  Heart is not 
enlarged.
ABDOMEN:
HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogeneous attenuation 
throughout. 
There is no evidence of focal lesions within the limitations of 
an unenhanced
scan.  There is no evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic 
biliary
dilatation.  The gallbladder is within normal limits.
PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, 
without evidence of
focal lesions within the limitations of an unenhanced scan.  
There is no
pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic 
stranding.
SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, 
without
evidence of focal lesions.
ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size 
and shape.
URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size.  There is 
no evidence
of focal renal lesions within the limitations of an unenhanced 
scan.  There is
no hydronephrosis.  There is no nephrolithiasis.  There is no 
perinephric
abnormality.
GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is collapsed.  The small bowel 
loops are largely
decompressed.  The colon and rectum are within normal limits.  
There is no
free fluid.
PELVIS: The bladder is collapsed around a Foley catheter and 
contains small
amount of air is likely iatrogenic.  There is a 
ventriculoperitoneal shunt
that terminates deep in the pelvis with a small adjacent free 
fluid (2:67).
REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The uterus is grossly unremarkable.  There 
are no adnexal
masses.
LYMPH NODES: There is no retroperitoneal or mesenteric 
lymphadenopathy.  There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Moderate 
atherosclerotic
disease is noted.
BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or 
acute fracture. 
There are multilevel degenerative changes in the spine.  There 
is moderate
compression deformity of the T11 vertebral body with 
vertebroplasty changes.
SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal 
limits.
 
IMPRESSION:
1. No acute intra-abdominal process or evidence of infection 
within
limitations of a noncontrast study.
2. Small amount of simple free fluid in the deep pelvis at the 
tip of the VP
shunt.
3. Trace pleural effusions, right greater than left, with mild 
adjacent
atelectasis.
 
___ TTE
The left atrial volume index is normal. The estimated right 
atrial pressure is ___ mmHg. There is mild (non-obstructive) 
focal hypertrophy of the basal septum. The left ventricular 
cavity size is normal. Regional left ventricular wall motion is 
normal. There is considerable beat-to-beat variability of the 
left ventricular ejection fraction due to an irregular 
rhythm/premature beats. Quantitative (biplane) LVEF = 63 %. The 
estimated cardiac index is normal (>=2.5L/min/m2). Right 
ventricular chamber size and free wall motion are normal. The 
number of aortic valve leaflets cannot be determined. No masses 
or vegetations are seen on the aortic valve. There is no aortic 
valve stenosis. No aortic regurgitation is seen. The mitral 
valve leaflets are structurally normal. No masses or vegetations 
are seen on the mitral valve, but cannot be fully excluded due 
to suboptimal image quality. No mitral regurgitation is seen. No 
masses or vegetations are seen on the tricuspid valve, but 
cannot be fully excluded due to suboptimal image quality. The 
estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure is normal. There is 
an anterior space which most likely represents a prominent fat 
pad. 

IMPRESSION: Suboptimal image quality. No echocardiographic 
evidence of endocarditis in a technically limited study. If 
clinically indicated, a transesophageal echocardiogram may 
better assess for valvular vegetations. Focal basal hypertrophy 
with preserved biventricular systolic function. 

___ LIVER US
LIVER: The hepatic parenchyma appears within normal limits. The 
contour of the
liver is smooth. There is no focal liver mass. The main portal 
vein is patent
with hepatopetal flow. There is no ascites.
BILE DUCTS: There is no intrahepatic biliary dilation. The CHD 
measures 3 mm.
GALLBLADDER: There is no evidence of stones or gallbladder wall 
thickening.
PANCREAS: The imaged portion of the pancreas appears within 
normal limits,
without masses or pancreatic ductal dilation, with portions of 
the pancreatic
tail obscured by overlying bowel gas.
SPLEEN:  Normal echogenicity, measuring 12.5 cm.
KIDNEYS:  Limited views of the right kidney show no 
hydronephrosis.
RETROPERITONEUM:  The visualized portions of aorta and IVC are 
within normal
limits. 
IMPRESSION: 
Unremarkable abdominal ultrasound.

___ RENAL US
The right kidney measures 9.8 cm. The left kidney measures 9.7 
cm. There is no
hydronephrosis, stones, or masses bilaterally.  Normal cortical 
echogenicity
and corticomedullary differentiation are seen bilaterally.
The urinary bladder is collapsed on a Foley catheter.
IMPRESSION: 
Normal renal ultrasound.

___ HEAD
The right VP shunt catheter results in a large amount of 
susceptibility
artifact overlying the right frontal and parietal lobes.  Images 
also limited
by motion artifact.
 
MRI BRAIN:
Allowing for obscuration of large portions of the right frontal 
and parietal
lobes by susceptibility artifact from the right-sided VP shunt 
catheter, there
is no evidence for acute infarction or unexplained blood 
products in the
visualized portion of the brain parenchyma.
 
The VP shunt catheter enters the frontal horn of the right 
lateral ventricle
and terminates at the septum pellucidum, unchanged compared to 
___. 
Compared to ___, the ventricles have substantially 
increased in
size, and are also minimally larger than on the earlier ___ CT. 
Hypodense subdural collections seen along the cerebral 
hemispheres on the
___ CT have resolved.  Small amount of right greater 
than left
retrocerebellar fluid is unchanged compared to ___ and 
___, compatible with ___ cisterna magna versus arachnoid cyst.
 
Confluent periventricular T2 hyperintensity has slightly 
progressed since the
___ MRI.  Multiple discrete and confluent foci of T2 
hyperintensity in
the deep and subcortical white matter of the cerebral 
hemispheres have also
progressed since the ___ MRI.  T2 hyperintensity in right 
greater than
left pons is unchanged.  These findings are nonspecific but 
usually sequela of
chronic small vessel ischemic disease in this age group, though 
the
periventricular T2 hyperintensity could also be secondary to 
transependymal
CSF migration in a patient with hydrocephalus.
 
Mild prominence of the sulci is again seen, indicating 
age-related parenchymal
volume loss.  Major vascular flow voids are grossly preserved.
 
Status post bilateral cataract surgery.  Mild mucosal thickening 
in the
ethmoid air cells and sphenoid sinuses.  Small amount of fluid 
in the sphenoid
sinuses may be secondary to prolonged supine positioning in the 
inpatient
setting, but please correlate clinically.
 
MRA NECK:
The study is markedly degraded by motion artifact.  Mediastinal 
portions of
the common carotid and vertebral arteries are not well assessed. 
 Cervical
portions of the vertebral arteries appear grossly patent.  
Vertebral artery is
dominant.  Apparent filling defects within bilateral carotid 
bulbs could
represent intrinsic artifacts of the 2D technique versus 
atherosclerotic
plaque.  Any associated stenosis cannot be quantified on this 
exam.
 
MRA BRAIN:
Intracranial internal carotid and vertebral arteries, and 
proximal courses of
their major branches, demonstrate no evidence for flow-limiting 
stenosis. 
More distal middle cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries 
appears slightly
irregular, but this could well be secondary to motion artifacts. 
 The left
vertebral artery is dominant, and the non dominant right 
vertebral artery
terminates as ___.  There is no evidence for an aneurysm larger 
than 3 mm;
evaluation for small aneurysms is limited by motion artifact.
IMPRESSION:
1. Motion limited exam.
2. Allowing for extensive susceptibility artifact from the 
right-sided VP
shunt catheter, which obscures large portions of the right 
frontal and
parietal lobes, there is no evidence for acute infarction or 
unexplained blood
products in the visualized brain parenchyma.
3. Stable position of the VP shunt catheter.  Compared to 
___, the
ventricles have increased in size (now minimally larger than in 
___, and bilateral hemispheric subdural effusions have 
resolved.
4. Progression of T2 signal abnormalities in the supratentorial 
white matter,
and unchanged T2 hyperintensities in the pons, which are 
nonspecific though
likely sequela of chronic small vessel ischemic disease in this 
age group. 
Periventricular abnormalities may also reflect sequela of 
transependymal CSF
flow in a patient with hydrocephalus.
5. Markedly motion degraded 2D time-of-flight neck MRA 
demonstrates apparent
filling defects within bilateral carotid bulbs, which could 
represent
intrinsic artifacts of the 2D  technique versus atherosclerotic 
plaque.  Any
associated stenosis cannot be quantified on this exam.
6. Motion limited brain MRA demonstrates no evidence for 
flow-limiting
stenosis involving the intracranial internal carotid and 
vertebral arteries,
and proximal courses of the major branches.  Evaluation of the 
more distal MCA
and PCA branches is technically limited.

___ MRI SPINE
1. There are 12 rib-bearing vertebrae, 5 lumbar-type vertebrae, 
and a nearly
completely sacralized L5.
2. Chronic T11 burst fracture with retropulsion, causing 
moderate spinal canal
narrowing with partial effacement of CSF around the ventral cord 
at T11-T12,
mild spinal canal narrowing at T10-T11, and moderate to severe 
bilateral
neural foraminal narrowing at T11-T12 and T10-T11.  No cord 
signal
abnormality.
3. Degenerative changes and epidural lipomatosis in the lumbar 
spine cause
severe narrowing of the thecal sac at L2-L3 with severe crowding 
of the
intrathecal nerve roots, moderate to severe narrowing of the 
thecal sac with
crowding of the intrathecal nerve roots at L3-L4, and moderate 
narrowing of

You make take Tylenol (Acetaminophen) 650mg every 6 hours as

over-the-counter and prescription medications contain Tylenol 
(acetaminophen) and you should never take more than 3000mg 
daily.  If your pain is poorly controlled with this regimen, you 
need to notify us.

It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart with pillows 
every ___ hours throughout the day and night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your legs 
elevated

appetite should return with time.

strength and assist in wound healing

softener if taking pain medication.

rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area 
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 1 
week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications (if 
you are taking narcotic pain medications)

Discharge Instructions:
Mr. ___,
It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___ 
___.  You were admitted to the hospital after surgery 
on your leg.   This surgery was done to improve blood flow to 
your leg.  After the blood flow was improved, we removed the 
unhealthy tissue from your ___ toe. You tolerated the procedure 
well and are now ready to be discharged from the hospital.   
Please follow the recommendations below to ensure a speedy and 
uneventful recovery.

Vascular Leg Surgery Discharge Instructions
What to except:

It is normal feel tired for ___ weeks after your surgery
It is normal to have leg swelling.  Keep your leg elevated as 
much as possible.  This will decrease the swelling. 
Your leg will feel tired and sore.   This usually passes 
within a few weeks.
Your incision will be sore, slightly raised, and pink.  Any 
drainage should decrease or stop with in the first 2 weeks. 
If you are home, you will likely receive a visit from a 
Visiting Nurse ___.  Members of your health care team will 
discuss this with you before you go home.   

Medications:
Before you leave the hospital, you will be given a list of all 
the medicine you should take at home.  If a medication that you 
normally take is not on the list or a medication that you do not 
take is on the list please discuss it with the team!  

It is very important that you take Aspirin every day!  You 
should never stop this medication before checking with your 
surgeon

Pain Management:
It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following surgery.  
This pain is often described as soreness. 
You may take Tylenol (acetaminophen ) as needed for pain.   
You will also receive a prescription for stronger pain medicine, 
 if the Tylenol doesnt work, take prescription medicine. 
Narcotic pain medication can be very constipating, please also 
take a stool softner such as Colace.   If constipation becomes a 
problem, your pharmacist can suggest additional over the counter 
medications. 
Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before your 
pain gets to severe. 
Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain 
is getting worse instead of better, please contact your surgeon. 


Activity:
Do not drive until your surgeon says it is okay.  In general, 
driving is not allowed until
-the staples in your leg have been taken out
-your leg feels strong
-you have stopped taking pain medication and feel you could 
respond in an emergency
Try not to go up and downstairs frequently and ambulate only 
essential distance until your toe incision is fully healed and 
you are back to your usual strength.
Avoid things that may constrict blood flow or put pressure on 
your incision, such as tight shoes, socks or knee highs.
Do not take a tub bath or swim until your staples are removed 
and your wound is healed. 
When you sit, keep your leg elevated to reduce swelling.
If swelling in your leg is getting worse, lie down with your 
leg up on a pillows.  If your swelling continues, please call 
your surgeon.  You may be instructed to use special elastic 
bandages or stockings.
Try not to sit in the same position for a long while.  For 
example, ___ go on a long car ride. 
You may go outside.  But avoid traveling long distances until 
you see your surgeon at your next visit. 
You may resume sexual activity after your incisions are well 
healed.

Your incision

Your incision may be slightly red around the stitches or 
staples.  This is normal.
It is normal to have a small amount of clear or light red 
fluid coming from your incision.
This will decrease and stop in a few days.  If it does not stop, 
or if you have a lot of fluid coming out., please call your 
surgeon.
You may shower 48 hours after your surgery.  Do not let the 
shower spray right on the incision,  Let the soapy water run 
over the incision, then rinse.  Gently pat the area dry.  Do not 
scrub the incision,  Do not apply ointment or lotions to the 
incision.
You do not need to cover the incision if there is no drainage, 
 If there is a small amount of drainage, put a small sterile 
gauze or Bandaid over the incison.
It is normal to feel a firm ridge along the incision,  This 
will go away as your wound heals. 
Avoid direct sun exposure to the incision area for 6 months.  
This will help keep the scar from becoming discolored.
Over ___ months, your incision will fade and become less 
prominent.

Diet and Bowels
It is normal to have a decreased appetite.  Your appetite will 
return over time.   Follow a well-balanced, health healthy diet, 
without too much salt and fat. 
Prescription pain medicine might make you constipated.  If 
needed, you may take a stool softener (such as Colace) or gentle 
laxative (ask your pharmacist for recommendations).
Drinking more fluid may also help.
If you go 48 hours without a bowel movement, or having pain 
moving your bowels, call your primary care physician.

with pain at the surgical site and was taken to the OR for I&D 
with washout of abscess. During her hospital stay the patient's 
cultures grew out MSSA and a PICC line was placed on ___ 
for intravenous Ancef therapy at home for 6 weeks (until ___

.

Chief Complaint:
Nonunion C45
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
Stage 1
1. Exploration of spinal fusion C4-C5.
2. Removal of hardware C4-C5.
3. Open deep biopsy, bone.
4. C4 partial corpectomy.
5. C5 vertebral body partial excision, removal of intrinsic
    lesion.
6. Allograft for fusion.
7. C4-C5 arthrodesis.

Stage 2:
1. Exploration of spinal fusion C4-C5, C5-C6, C6-C7.
2. C4-C5 bilateral hemilaminotomy.
3. Posterior cervical fusion C4-C5.
4. Instrumentation C4 to C5.
5. Allograft for fusion.
6. Iliac crest bone graft for fusion.

 
History of Present Illness:
In summary, she is a ___ female who underwent anterior
cervical discectomy and fusion, ___, for treatment of disc
segment disease.  She developed postoperative infection,
osteomyelitis, requiring suppressive antibiotics.  For that
reason in part she wants to become a candidate for hardware
removal with a goal of eradicating her infection.

We did perform a CT scan for her on ___ to assess the
status of her fusion.  She also want flexion and extension
radiographs.  Both her CT scan and flexion and extension
radiographs are most consistent with a nonunion.  Since she did
not have a healed spinal fusion, revision surgery treatment will
require a two-staged approach.

We discussed at length the surgical strategy and also the
rationale for surgery.  We discussed the alternatives, risks and
benefits of both surgical and ongoing nonsurgical care.  With 
the
goal of eradicating infection, ultimately hopefully desisting 
the
use of antibiotics, she has elected to undergo surgical
treatment.

This would be a two-staged approach.

The first stage would be anterior cervical hardware removal at
C4-C5 with debridement of the surgical site.  This would then
allow cultures to also be taken, and first to follow her
inflammatory markers as an inpatient following that surgery.  
She
would then be treated with postoperative antibiotics.  If
postoperative antibiotics offer to have a normal decline in her
CRP trend, we may then pursue posterior spinal fusion with iliac
crest bone graft in the same hospitalization.  If further
antibiotics are required, with infectious disease consultation 
as
an inpatient, then we would do a second staged surgery for her
some weeks in the future after the goals of _____ sepsis have
been achieved in order to decrease the risk of potential wound
infection in her posterior cervical spine.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to ___ after 
you lost consciousness and fell.  You sustained left-sided rib 
fractures and a small traumatic puncture, called a pneumothorax, 
to your left lung.  You had an epidural placed to achieve pain 
control.  Your rib fractures and pneumothorax will heal on their 
own.

You are now ready to be discharged home to continue your 
recovery.  Please note the following discharge instructions:

Rib Fractures:

* Your injury caused left-sided rib fractures which can cause 
severe pain and subsequently cause you to take shallow breaths 
because of the pain.
 
* You should take your pain medication as directed to stay ahead 
of the pain otherwise you won't be able to take deep breaths. If 
the pain medication is too sedating take half the dose and 
notify your physician.
 
* Pneumonia is a complication of rib fractures.  In order to 
decrease your risk you must use your incentive spirometer 4 
times every hour while awake.  This will help expand the small 
airways in your lungs and assist in coughing up secretions that 
pool in the lungs.
 
* You will be more comfortable if you use a cough pillow to hold 
against your chest and guard your rib cage while coughing and 
deep breathing.
 
* Symptomatic relief with ice packs or heating pads for short 
periods may ease the pain.
 
* Narcotic pain medication can cause constipation therefore you 
should take a stool softener twice daily and increase your fluid 
and fiber intake if possible.
 
* Do NOT smoke
 
* If your doctor allows, non-steroidal ___ drugs 
are very effective in controlling pain ( ie, Ibuprofen, Motrin, 
Advil, Aleve, Naprosyn) but they have their own set of side 
effects so make sure your doctor approves.
 
* Return to the Emergency Room right away for any acute 
shortness of breath, increased pain or crackling sensation 
around your ribs (crepitus).

General Discharge Instructions:

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. Avoid lifting 
weights greater than ___ lbs until you follow-up with your 
surgeon.
Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old man with history of end-stage liver 
disease, hepatitis C,  anuric ESRD on HD via LUE fistula, CAD 
(s/p BMS x 2) who presented to ___ with acute massive 
upper GI bleeding. Patient was transferred to ___, intubated 
for airway protection and transferred to the MICU for further 
treatment. EGD showed grade IV bleeding varices requiring 6 
bands. Patient subsequently developed signs of rebleeding, 
hypotension and underwent ___ placement and emergent TIPS 
procedure. Patient became progressively more hypotensive with 
stable hematocrit and no improvement despite blood transfusion, 
3 vasopressors. Patient developed refractory hypotension and 
worsening acidosis. He subsequently had a PEA arrest and passed 
away with his wife and 2 daughters at bedside. 

MICU COURSE:
============

#Massive upper GI bleed:
Patient presented with acute massive GI bleed. Hepatology 
performed EGD with banding of several large actively bleeding 
grade IV esophageal varices. Patient subsequently showed 
evidence of re-bleeding with oozing of blood from around his ET 
tube and hypotension. A ___ tube was placed to tamponade 
the bleed, IV antibiotics were started for potential sepsis, 1U 
PRBC transfused, and the patient was taken urgently to the ___ 
suite for TIPS procedure. During the procedure patient had 
worsening hypotension and acidosis requiring increasing doses of 
vasopressors. There were no procedural complications and hepatic 
wedge pressure improved. When patient returned to the ICU he had 
evidence of worsening acidosis, rising lactate, and worsening 
hypotension despite 4 vasopressors. At that time patient's wife, 
daughters, and extended family agreed that CPR would not be 
indicated and would not help to improve his underlying 
condition, he was then made DNR. Over the course of the evening 
patient became more acidotic with minimal improvement despite 
sodium bicarbonate, hyperventilation on the ventilator. Patient 
then became progressively more hypotensive despite the 
vasopressors while hematocrit remained stable. Patient's wife 
and daughters came to his bedside, vasopressors were weaned off 
and patient had PEA arrest. Time of death 0614 AM.   
 
#Cirrhosis:
___ Class B, secondary to Hepatitis C. No history of 
previous decompensated cirrhosis, patient was actively on the 
liver-kidney transplant list at ___.

FSGS. Patient was too hemodynamically unstable to receive HD 
during admission, CRRT not indicated with no severe electrolyte 
abnormalities.

showing peaked T-waves. Given calcium, insulin, dextrose, and 
albuterol nebulizer in the ED with decrease in K to less than 5 
and normalization of T-waves.

Patient was admitted in the setting of his obstructing stone and 
poorly controlled pain. He was given IVF and pain control and 
made NPO after midnight. On hospital day two he underwent an 
uncomplicated cystoscopy, left ureteroscopy, laser lithotripsy, 
retrograde pyelogram, and ureteral stent placement. Please see 
the seperately dictated operative report for details. Afterwards 
patient remained afebrile and well-appearing. Pain was well 
controlled on oral pain meds. He tolerated diet advancement. He 
ambulated without issue. He was given instructions and

-You can expect to see occasional blood in your urine and to 
possibly experience some urgency and frequency over the next 
month;  this may be related to the passage of stone fragments or 
the indwelling ureteral stent (if there is one).

-The kidney stone may or may not have been removed AND/or there 
may fragments/others still in the process of passing.

-You may experience some pain associated with spasm of your 
ureter.; This is normal. Take the narcotic pain medication as 
prescribed if additional pain relief is needed.

-Ureteral stents MUST be removed or exchanged and therefore it 
is IMPERATIVE that you follow-up as directed. 

-Do not lift anything heavier than a phone book (10 pounds)

aspirin until you see your urologist in follow-up

even though you may also be taking Tylenol/Acetaminophen. You 
may alternate these medications for pain control. For pain 
control, try TYLENOL FIRST, then ibuprofen, and then take the 
narcotic pain medication as prescribed if additional pain relief 
is needed.

stool (dark, tarry stools)

that will help with the "burning" pain you may experience when 
voiding. This medication may turn your urine bright orange.

and constipation related to narcotic pain medication.

stool softener, NOT a laxative, and available over the counter.

use this medication.

fluids to keep hydrated

Foley catheter is in place.

Brief Hospital Course:
Pt underwent laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy on ___.  He 
recovered uneventfully.  On POD1, he was advanced to sips.  His 
Foley was d/c'd (UA was negative), and he voided.  On POD2, he 
passed flatus and was advanced to regular diet.  At the time of 
discharge, he was afebrile with stable vital signs, his pain was 
controlled with PO medications, he was tolerating a diet, and he 
was ambulating independently.

Discharge Instructions:
S/P Laparoscopic Colectomy

You were admitted to the hospital after a laparoscopic sigmoid 
colectomy for surgical management of your diverticulitis.  You 
have recovered from this procedure well and you are now ready to 
return home. Samples from your colon were taken and this tissue 
has been sent to the pathology department for analysis. You will 
receive these pathology results at your follow-up appointment. 
If there is an urgent need for the surgeon to contact you 
regaurding these results they will contact you before this time. 
You have tolerated a regular diet, passing gas and your pain is 
controlled with pain medications by mouth. You may return home 
to finish your recovery.

Please monitor your bowel function closely. You may or may not 
have had a bowel movement prior to your discharge which is 
acceptable, however it is important that you have a bowel 
movement in the next ___ days. After anesthesia it is not 
uncommon for patients to have some decrease in bowel function 
but you should not have prolonged constipation. Some loose stool 
and passing of small amounts of dark, old appearing blood are 
explected however, if you notice that you are passing bright red 
blood with bowel movments or having loose stool without 
improvement please call the office or go to the emergency room 
if the symptoms are severe. If you are taking narcotic pain 
medications there is a risk that you will have some 
constipation. Please take an over the counter stool softener 
such as Colace, and if the symptoms does not improve call the 
office. If you have any of the following symptoms please call 
the office for advice or go to the emergency room if severe: 
increasing abdominal distension, increasing abdominal pain, 
nausea, vomiting, inability to tolerate food or liquids, 
prolonges loose stool, or constipation. 

You have ___ laparoscopic surgical incisions on your abdomen 
which are closed with internal surtures and the skin glue 
dermabond. These are healing well however it is important that 
you monitor these areas for signs and symptoms of infection 
including: increasing redness of the incision lines, 
white/gree/yellow/malodorous drainage, increased pain at the 
incision, increased warmth of the skin at the incision, or 
swelling of the area. Please call the office if you develop any 
of these symptoms or a fever. You may go to the emergency room 
if your symptoms are severe. You may shower, pat the incisions 
dry with a towel do not rub. The small incisions may be left 
open to the air. If closed with steri-strips, these will fall 
off on their own, please do not remove them. Please no baths or 
swimming for 6 weeks after surgery unless told otherwise by Dr. 
___.

No heavy lifting greater than 6 lbs for until your first 
post-operative visit after surgery. Please no strenuous activity 
until this time unless instructed otherwise by Dr. ___.

Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care! Our hope 
is that you will have a quick return to your life and usual 
activities. Good luck!

Surgery

History of Present Illness:
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  Mr. ___ is a ___
gentleman who comes with the above chief complaint.  He has an
extensive history as in regards to that leg as well as 
documented
in the EMR.  Briefly, he had a fracture of the distal tibia,
fibula, complicated by wound infection, requiring debridement,
bone grafting and subsequent removal of hardware.  It appears
that he is infection free but has developed significant pain in
his ankle and hindfoot secondary to posttraumatic arthritis and
comes to me in this regard.  He is a ___.  He has 
tried
an ankle brace, shoewear modification and Aircast boot 
offloading
with a cane and crutches as well as Advil and complains of ___nd ___ pain with activity, made worse with
standing or walking.  He works at the ___ in
___.  He denies any paresthesias or dysesthesias, but does
report some slightly decreased sensation to light touch in that
extremity.  He is not diabetic.  He does not smoke.  He is a
___.

Past Medical History:  High blood pressure, depression, anxiety,
arthritis.

Past Surgical History:  As above.

Medications:  Verapamil, amitriptyline, multivitamin, Excedrin,
Advil, Tylenol.

Allergies:  No known drug allergies.

Family History:  Positive for cancer, diabetes, heart disease, 
GI
problems, and joint disease.

Social History:  Social ETOH.

Review of Systems:  As documented by the patient and reviewed by
myself.

On physical examination, he is in no acute distress and
cooperative.  He is a Caucasian male appearing his stated age 
who
is oriented with no labored breathing.  He has a reasonably
aligned hindfoot, although he is in some hindfoot valgus.  He 
has
a significant antalgia to his gait.  He has well-healed surgical
scars, and normal coloration.  There is no induration or
fluctuance or drainage.  He is exquisitely point tender across
the anterior ankle joint line with some tenderness in the sinus
tarsi area.  He is grossly sensation intact to light touch and 
is
well perfused.

Radiographic Examination:  Multiple views of the ankle
demonstrate a healed fracture of the distal tibia.  There is no
overt evidence of infection.  He has post-traumatic changes of
the ankle and subtalar joint.

Impression and Plan:  I had a long talk with ___ in the 
office
today.  He has post-traumatic arthritis of the ankle with some
symptomology from the subtalar joint after his previous injury. 
I do not see any evidence of infection radiographically and
clinically.  I reviewed his recent blood work and his white 
blood
cell count and inflammatory markers are essentially within 
normal
limits.  We have discussed conservative treatments for this,
which include some of the modalities, he is trying in addition 
to
cortisone.  After informed consent was obtained, I gave him an
injection 2 mL of Kenalog 40 and 2% plain lidocaine into the
ankle joint, which he tolerated well.  He is very much concerned
about his employment at ___ as well as the need
for possibly a desk job as opposed to being a ___.  We
have discussed this in detail.  Furthermore, I have explained to
him that arthrodesis of the hindfoot would require a lengthy
period of nonweightbearing recovery.  He understands this.  He
would like to think about his options.  He will contact me
shortly.

I do think that given his symptomology, he would require a TTC
arthrodesis.

Sincerely,

___ MD

The patient presented as a same day admission for surgery. The

which the patient tolerated 

 
well. For full details of the procedure please see the 

 
separately dictated operative report.

 

 
Post operatively, she was admitted for IV pain control.  His

 
pain was well controlled on PO medications and he was

At the time of discharge the patient's pain was well controlled 

 
with oral medications, dressings were clean/dry/intact, and the 

 
patient was voiding/moving bowels spontaneously. The patient 

 
will be discharged on Aspirin for DVT prophylaxis. The patient 

 
will follow up in two weeks with Dr. ___ routine. A

 
thorough discussion was had with the patient regarding the 

 
diagnosis and expected post-discharge course including reasons 

 
to call the office or return to the hospital, and all questions 

 
were answered. The patient was also given written instructions 

 
concerning precautionary instructions and the appropriate 

 
follow-up care. The patient expressed readiness for discharge.

Prescription refills or changes cannot be addressed after normal 

business hours or on weekends.

PAIN CONTROL:
- You may or may not have had a nerve block depending on the 
type of surgery. This will likely wear off later in the evening 
and it is normal to have increased pain when the nerve block 
wears off. Please take your prescribed pain medications as 
directed with food prior to the nerve block wearing off.
- Stay ahead of the pain!
- Narcotic pain medications can cause constipation. Please take 
a stool softener while taking these and drink plenty of water.
- Please plan ahead! If you are running out of your medication 
prior to your followup appointment please call during business 
hours with a ___ day notice. Prescription refills or changes 
cannot be addressed after normal business hours or on weekends.

- You will likely have swelling after surgery. Please keep the 
foot elevated on ___ pillows at all times possible. You can 
apply a dry icebag on top of your dressing for 20 minutes at a 
time as often as you like.

on your operated extremity until you come back for your first 
postoperative visit.

- It is not unusual to have a little bloody staining through 
your dressing. However please call the office for any concerns.

- You have been instructed to take medication in order to help 
prevent blood clots after surgery. Please take an aspirin 325 mg 

every day unless you have been specifically prescribed a 
different medication by me. If there is some reason why you 
cannot take aspirin please notify my office.

DRIVING:
- My recommendation is that you should not drive if you:

side

transmission (stick shift)

Name:  ___.              Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___

History of Present Illness:
Ms. ___ is a ___ female who presented with signs and 
symptoms concerning for progressive reflux. She wished strongly 
to be off her PPI medication. She had standard preoperative 
workup, including manometry, pH, endoscopy, and barium swallow. 
All the tests demonstrated abnormal motility of her esophagus. 
She was reviewed at a motility meeting with Dr. ___. Given her 
poor motility, the decision was made that she would have, at the 
most, a Dor or Toupet partial fundoplication for her GERD, given 
that she had significant reflux based on her pH study and 
___ score. The findings of the motility meeting were 
discussed with her in detail as well as the risks and rationale 
for repair, the risks including bleeding, infection, bowel 
injury, reoperation, perforation, conversion to open, dysphagia, 
pain, and scars were discussed in detail. She consented fully.

resolved

Brief Hospital Course:
Dates of hospitalization: ___ - ___:

Ms. ___ was admitted to the ___ Surgery service on 
___ after an elective and uneventful laparoscopic repair of 
hiatal hernia and partial fundoplication for surgical management 
of symptoms of gastric reflux. The reader is referred to the 
operative note for details. 

Neuro: Post-operatively, the patient received Dilaudid PCA and 
IV Tylenol with good effect and adequate pain control. When 
tolerating oral intake, the patient was transitioned to oral 
liquid/crushable pain medications.

CV: Vital signs were closely monitored and patient remained 
stable from a cardiovascular standpoint for the rest of the 
hospitalization. 

Pulmonary: The patient initially had an increased O2 requirement 
which resolved with incentive spirometry, and nebulizations. 
Respiratory toilet was encouraged with eventual wean off oxygen 
prior to discharge.

GI/GU: Post-operatively, the patient was given IV fluids until 
tolerating sufficient oral intake. On POD1, her nasogastric tube 
was removed, patient underwent swallow study which showed no 
leak. Her diet was advanced to clears, which was tolerated well. 
All oral medications including her home meds were administered 
in either liquid form or ODT form and a few medications were 
crushed. Proton-pump inhibitor therapy was resumed. Foley was 
removed on POD 0, and she voided without any difficulty 
afterwards. Intake and output were closely monitored.

ID: The patient's temperature was closely watched for signs of 
infection, of which there were none. 

Prophylaxis: The patient received subcutaneous heparin during 
this stay, and was encouraged to get up and ambulate as early as 
possible. 

At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
hemodynamically stable, tolerating clears, ambulating, voiding 
without assistance, and pain was well 
controlled. Patient was recommended to continue clears for 2 
more days and then advance to full liquids.
